header.tag_why: The CFO compared two rate lines and saw 'the same thing', because nothing from us put a Fernbrook-specific cost on the failed orders, even though Farah offered to build it and Lucy asked for a business case.

evidence.excerpt: She said about one in twelve online orders was failing at the payment step, and it was worse on the big baskets.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Her number. Off their own dashboard.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: she couldn't get a straight answer from the processor on why.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: "we do all the work to get someone to buy a four-thousand-dollar greenhouse and then the card says no."
evidence.label: quote

trigger.insight: The customer arrived with a quantified problem from their own dashboard and no explanation from their processor. The raw material for a cost-of-failure case was there from the first call, but the story never got turned into money for the person who signs. The 'no straight answer' gap was our opening, and it ended up as a nice conversation with the champion.
trigger.messaging: Open with the cost of failed big-ticket orders in the buyer's own dashboard numbers and an explanation of why they fail, instead of a generic acceptance claim.

evidence.excerpt: The CFO, Martin. Lucy was the champion, she wanted it, IT was fine with it. Martin said no.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Lucy told me. I never met him.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Lucy said he doesn't take vendor meetings and she'd carry it.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Martin and the controller. I wasn't in the room. Lucy presented it.
evidence.label: fact

decider.insight: Everything we know about the decision comes through Lucy, who said it was a formality right before it failed, so her read of Martin was wrong. The case went to a CFO who does not take vendor meetings, carried only by a champion with no finance-grade material from us. We never tested whether Martin saw anything beyond the one-pager.
decider.messaging: Give champions a CFO-ready leave-behind that works without us in the room, since some finance buyers will never take a vendor meeting.

evidence.excerpt: when the bank heard, they came back and sharpened the rate.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: No new product, nothing. Just a better rate.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Up to then Lucy was asking about declines. Why big orders fail, what we'd do about it.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: After the bank came back, every email was the rate.
evidence.label: fact

competitor.insight: Per Lucy, the incumbent's whole response was a lower rate, and that was enough to turn a conversation about declines into a conversation about rate. Lucy's questions moved from why big orders fail to asking us to do better on the rate. Our decline story did not hold once price became the frame.
competitor.messaging: When an incumbent counters on rate, answer with a total-cost comparison covering rate, gateway fees, chargeback handling and the value of failed orders, not a matching discount.

evidence.excerpt: Lucy loved the checkout. And the decline piece.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Lucy was nodding the whole way.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Silence, honestly, nothing bombed. It was a good cycle. We lost on price.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: The customer stories. The average uplift.
evidence.label: fact

message.insight: The only reaction reported is Lucy's, and it did not travel to the person who decided. 'Nothing bombed' sits oddly next to a thread that collapsed into rate talk, so the decline message landed with the champion but failed to survive the CFO review. Whether Martin reacted to any part of our pitch is unknown.
message.messaging: Stop leading with the average-uplift line in M4 and pair the decline explanation with a number the customer can check against their own orders.

evidence.excerpt: he's not going to pay more for the same thing.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: The controller did a one-pager for Martin. Our rate, their rate, side by side.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Our quote.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: And Martin would still have been looking at a page that said same rate, so why move. So maybe not only the rate.
evidence.label: opinion

decided.insight: The decision document was a rate-versus-rate page with our quote as the only item from us, so we lost the comparison on a page we did not shape. The rep says price, but also admits that matching it might not have won, citing the same-rate page and IT's timing worry. The real failure is that nothing on the page made it not 'the same thing'.
decided.messaging: Structure every quote so it carries the customer-specific cost of the problem next to the rate, because the finance reader will compare whatever lines are on the page.

evidence.excerpt: Lucy asked once if we had something she could hand Martin. Like a one-page business case.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I sent her the deck and the pricing proposal.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Farah offered to run their declines. She wanted a three-month export so she could show what the failed orders were worth.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: it was the last two weeks of the quarter, and I didn't want to slow things down.
evidence.label: fact

gaps.insight: The gap was a choice, not a product limit: the champion asked for a business case and the SE offered to build one. The rep skipped it because of quarter-end pace and because Lucy seemed sold, then admitted nothing from us quantified the cost for Martin. The rep's 'we lost on price' also leaves out that we never tried to show the cost of not switching.
gaps.messaging: Turn the decline export into a standard early step that produces a one-page customer-specific business case, and make it a stage requirement in the sales process.

evidence.excerpt: "orders dying at the last step."
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: "the big baskets."
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: "we do all the work to get someone to buy a four-thousand-dollar greenhouse and then the card says no."
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: "Why would I pay more for the same thing."
evidence.label: quote

language.insight: Lucy describes a sales problem at the moment of payment, while our deck says declines and acceptance uplift. Martin's only reported words are about price parity. The two buyers use different vocabularies, and ours matches neither. Martin's words come only secondhand through Lucy and the rep.
language.messaging: Write decline copy in the buyer's terms, such as orders dying at the last step and the big baskets, and give the CFO a separate line about what failed big orders cost.

gaps.question: Which part of our pitch got a reaction, and which got silence?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Sam: after the bank's counter, what specifically did Lucy stop asking about, and did anyone besides Lucy react to our decline explanation?

gaps.question: If we had matched the price, would we have won? What else would have needed to be true?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Sam: you said yes, then said maybe not only the rate; which is it, and what did IT's worry about moving before spring actually hinge on?

gaps.question: So what did Martin have in front of him about what one in twelve orders was costing?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy (via Sam, or a customer call): what did you tell Martin about the failed orders, and what did he say about them?

gaps.question: Who made the final call, and how do you know?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy: what did Martin say beyond 'the same thing', and did the controller raise anything beyond the rate lines?

close.rep_takeaway: When a champion asks for something to hand the CFO and your SE offers to build it, build it, even at quarter-end. You told us Lucy was sold, but she wasn't the one signing, and the CFO only ever saw two rate lines.
